1100.title: Baptism, deeper
1100.hook: some say baptism brings new birth; others that it signs a birth already happened
1100.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptize infants as well as adults, by pouring, sprinkling or immersion; Baptist and other believers' churches baptize people who profess faith, usually by full immersion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the priesthood of all believers, from the altar to the cobbler's bench. Your line was a royal priesthood.

It's night, and a respected teacher named Nicodemus has come to find Jesus quietly. He opens politely. Jesus skips the politeness and says a man must be born again to see the kingdom of God. Nicodemus is baffled, and says so: "How can a man be born when he is old?" Climb back into your mother? Jesus answers with two elements: water and Spirit. Since then, water has been poured over infants at stone fonts, and grown adults have gone under in rivers. Day one hundred fifty-two met baptism two ways. Today, deeper: what does the water do?
screen: `HOW CAN A MAN BE BORN WHEN OLD?`

segments.voice: The answer: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Churches across the traditions baptize; the question is what the water does. One answer: baptism is God's own act, and in it God gives the new birth. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican teaching point to Paul's phrase to Titus, "the washing of regeneration," and read it as describing the font itself. That's one reason these churches baptize infants. A baby can't decide anything, and in their teaching that's the point: the gift comes first, and faith grows up inside it. A second answer: baptism is an outward sign of a new birth God gives by the Spirit through faith. Baptist and other believers' churches teach that a person is born again by trusting Christ, then baptized, usually by full immersion, as a public witness that it has already happened. So they baptize those old enough to say so. Presbyterian and Reformed churches take a third road: they baptize the infants of believers as a sign and seal of God's covenant promise, while teaching that the water doesn't work automatically. Now what they share. Paul, to the Romans: "we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Under the water, a burial. Out of it, a rising. Either way, the shape is the same: going down, and coming up, new.
screen: `BORN OF WATER AND OF THE SPIRIT.` · `GOD'S ACT: THE WASHING OF REGENERATION.` · `A SIGN OF A BIRTH ALREADY GIVEN.` · `A COVENANT SIGN AND SEAL.` · then, large: `BURIED WITH HIM, RAISED TO NEW LIFE.`

segments.voice: If you were baptized, bring it to mind, even if only from a photo or a story. If you weren't, bring to mind a beginning that mattered, a moment you went under in some way and came up different. Notice what in it was given to you, and what you chose. If you pray, give thanks for that beginning; if you don't, just rest in having begun.
Baptism. Being washed, buried and raised in water: for some churches the new birth itself, for others its sign.
Your line: born of water. A burial, and a rising. Until tomorrow.

1101.title: The Real Presence
1101.hook: Catholics teach bread and wine become Christ's body and blood; the Orthodox affirm the change and call it mystery
1101.howItsDone: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, bow or kneel before the consecrated host, and keep it in a tabernacle for adoration; Orthodox Christians receive the holy gifts in the Divine Liturgy, confessing a real change and calling it a mystery.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism, deeper: the new birth itself, or its sign and seal. Your line was born of water.

"This is an hard saying; who can hear it?" Many of his own disciples say it in the sixth chapter of John, in a synagogue in Capernaum. Jesus has just told them that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood, they have no life in them. Readers still argue over how he meant it. John says that from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Then Jesus turns to the twelve: "Will ye also go away?" Peter answers for them, honestly: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." He doesn't claim to understand. He stays.

Fast forward to the night before he died. Jesus takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and says: "Take, eat; this is my body." Then the cup: "this is my blood." Paul asks the Corinthians: "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" What does "is" mean at that table? Day one hundred fifty-three gave short answers; this takes two days. Today, two churches that answer: really, truly is. Catholics teach that at the consecration in the Mass, the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. Transubstantiation is the word Catholic councils used to name that change. It borrows an old distinction from philosophy: what a thing really is, its substance, and how it appears to the senses. The appearances of bread and wine remain: the taste, the color, the crumbs. But what it is has changed. That's why Catholics kneel or bow before the consecrated host, keep it in a tabernacle, and sit before it in silent adoration. Orthodox Christians also confess that the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood, but are wary of defining how. In the Divine Liturgy the change is prayed for: the priest asks the Holy Spirit to come down on the gifts. They call the sacraments mysteries, and they're content to leave this one there. Two traditions, one table, each holding its way with reverence. And Peter again: not now I understand, but to whom shall we go? In John's telling, faith can look like staying with words you can't fully explain.
screen: `THIS IS MY BODY.` · `CATHOLIC: SUBSTANCE CHANGED.` · `APPEARANCES OF BREAD REMAIN.` · `ORTHODOX: A REAL CHANGE, A MYSTERY.` · then, large: `TO WHOM SHALL WE GO?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you can't fully explain and can't quite dismiss: a love, a grief, a moment larger than itself, or, if you receive communion, the bread and the cup. Don't solve it; if it feels right, bow your head slightly, as people do at the altar. If you pray, offer that bow to God; if you don't, let it simply be respect.
Transubstantiation. The Catholic word for bread and wine becoming Christ's body and blood, while their appearances remain.
Your line: a holy mystery. Peter didn't understand it all, and still he stayed. See you tomorrow.

1102.title: Other views of the table
1102.hook: Lutherans: Christ truly present in, with and under; Calvin: spiritual feeding; Zwingli: memorial
1102.howItsDone: Lutheran, Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist and other Protestant churches all keep the Lord's Supper, under names like communion or the Lord's Supper, and they explain Christ's presence in it in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Real Presence: transubstantiation for Catholics, a holy mystery for the Orthodox. Your line was a holy mystery.

One table, one loaf, and a long argument about it. Paul says it happened on the night Jesus was betrayed. In Luke's telling, Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, hands it round, and adds a request: "this do in remembrance of me." Yesterday, Catholics and the Orthodox read his other words at that table, "Take, eat; this is my body." Today, three more chairs, each taking one small word in that sentence a different way. Is.

Start with Martin Luther, who held on hard to that little word. Lutherans teach that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. The bread stays bread, and Christ is really there, given into your hand. Lutherans don't explain how; they take the words as spoken. Then John Calvin, in Geneva. Calvin taught that believers truly feed on Christ, but by the Holy Spirit, who lifts them up to him, rather than by Christ's body coming down into the bread. Real food, received by faith. Reformed and Presbyterian churches stand in that line. Then Huldrych Zwingli, in Zurich. Zwingli read is as signifies, the way someone points at a photo and says, that's my grandmother. For him the meal is a memorial: the church remembers, gives thanks, and is joined together as one body. Baptist churches, among others, call the meal an ordinance: something Jesus commanded, done in remembrance. But remembering, in Paul, is more than thinking back. Passing the words on to Corinth, he adds: "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come." Remembering is something the church does, out loud, together. And when Paul scolds Corinth about the supper, the first trouble he names isn't theory. Some go hungry while others eat first. His fix is plain: "when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another." Wait for each other. These churches read the meal differently, and say so honestly. None of their views lets anyone skip that verse.

If there's bread nearby, pause before you eat and notice the many hands it came through: a field, a baker, a truck, a shelf. If someone is with you, offer them some first and wait until they have it; if you're alone, bring to mind one person you'd want at your table. If you pray, give thanks in words you already know; if you don't, let the pause itself be the thanks.
Other views of the table. Lutherans: Christ present in, with and under the bread. Calvin: feeding on Christ by the Spirit. Zwingli: a meal of remembrance.

1103.title: Mary across the churches
1103.hook: churches call Mary God-bearer; Catholics and Orthodox honor her highly; Protestants honor her as a model disciple
1103.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the rosary; Orthodox Christians sing hymns to the Theotokos in their services; Protestant churches read Mary's song, the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55), and honor her as a model of faith, especially around Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, other views of the table: in, with and under; fed by the Spirit; a meal of memory. Your line was do this in memory.

A young woman hurries into the hill country of Judea to see her cousin Elizabeth. Her name is Mary, and she is carrying news she can hardly explain. She barely gets through the door before Elizabeth, old and herself unexpectedly pregnant, cries out: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" The mother of my Lord. Christians have thought hard about that phrase, and one Greek title stands behind much of it.

Theotokos is Greek for God-bearer: the one who gave birth to God. That sounds bold, and it's meant to. But the title is really about her son. If the child she carried is one person, truly God and truly human, then the woman who bore him bore God. When this was argued in the early church, a council at Ephesus defended the title, and Orthodox and Catholic prayer still uses it. From there the churches honor her in different ways. Orthodox Christians sing hymns to the Theotokos and keep her icons close. Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the rosary, and teach that she was conceived without sin and taken up body and soul into heaven. Protestant churches generally don't pray to her, and don't hold those last teachings as doctrine. They honor her as the model disciple, who heard God's word and said, "be it unto me according to thy word." At a wedding in Cana, when the wine ran out, she told the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." She points away from herself, to him. Then there's her own song in Luke, the Magnificat: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." And a few lines later, the line behind today's carry: "from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed." A young woman from Nazareth says that about herself, and it's in every church's Bible. The churches argue over how to honor her. None of them disputes that she is blessed.

Open Luke chapter one at verse forty-six, Mary's song, in any Bible or on your phone, and read it slowly, once, noticing who goes up and who comes down: the proud scattered, the mighty put down from their seats, the lowly lifted, the hungry filled. Then sit with whichever line stays. If you pray, let her words rise as your own for a moment; if you don't, just let the song be heard.
Theotokos. Greek for God-bearer: Mary, the mother of the child Christians call truly God and truly human.
Your line: all generations call her blessed. A young woman's yes, still sung. Until tomorrow.

1104.title: Praying with the saints
1104.hook: Catholics and Orthodox ask the saints to pray for them; Protestant churches pray to God alone
1104.howItsDone: Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask saints, especially Mary, to pray for them, and keep saints' days through the year; Protestant Christians pray to God through Christ and ask fellow believers to pray for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary across the churches, and the Greek title Theotokos, God-bearer. Your line was all generations call her blessed.

Pray for me. People say it in hospital corridors, text it before a job interview, whisper it at a graveside. Paul asks the Romans to strive together with him in their prayers. James tells his readers, plainly, to pray one for another. On that much, the text is clear. The question comes when the person you'd ask has died. Can you ask a saint in heaven to pray for you, the way you'd ask a friend down the hall? The churches answer differently.

Intercession means praying on someone else's behalf, standing in for them before God. Paul urges it in his first letter to Timothy: "supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men." Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask the saints to pray for them. Their reasoning: those who died in Christ are alive in God, not gone. So asking Mary or Saint Peter to pray for you is like asking a friend who is now very near to God. They are careful to say this is not worship; worship belongs to God alone. They point to Revelation, where elders before the Lamb hold "golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints." Protestant churches, following the Reformers, direct prayer to God alone. They point to the same letter to Timothy, a few lines later: "there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Protestants still ask one another to pray, gladly. They keep those requests among the living, and bring everything else straight to God through Christ. Then there's a verse both sides read closely, in Hebrews. After a long roll call of faithful people, Abraham and Sarah, Moses and Rahab, it says: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." Catholics and Orthodox hear the saints praying alongside the living. Protestants hear a crowd of examples, lives that still testify. Either way, the next words, "let us run with patience," put the runner in a full stadium, not an empty one.

Bring to mind one person of faith whose life still speaks to you: Francis, or Peter, or Mary herself, or a grandmother who prayed every morning, a teacher who showed you patience. Recall one thing they did or said that you'd like to carry into your week, and hold it for a while. If you pray, thank God for that life; if you don't, say their name quietly, and keep the one thing.
Intercession. Praying on behalf of someone else. Every church here does it for the living; they differ on asking the saints to join in.
Your line: the cloud of witnesses. Pray one for another, as James puts it. Same time tomorrow.

1105.title: Images
1105.hook: Orthodox honor icons; Catholics statues; Reformed churches keep walls plain from the second commandment
1105.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians venerate icons at home and in church, often kissing them and lighting candles before them; Catholic churches hold statues, crucifixes and stained glass; Reformed churches keep their worship spaces plain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, intercession: praying for one another, and the question of asking the saints. Your line was the cloud of witnesses.

The walls of an Orthodox church look back at you. Christ, Mary, apostles and saints, painted in gold and deep color, face you from the walls and the screen before the altar. People coming in kiss the icons and light candles in front of them. Now step into a Reformed church: white walls, clear windows, a pulpit, a table, an open Bible, and very little else. Both rooms are built for prayer to the same God. Both were made to look that way on purpose.

Start with the commandment. In Exodus, God says: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above." And the next verse: don't bow down to them. Reformed churches count this as the second commandment, and they take it seriously: no images in worship, so nothing stands between the worshiper and the living God, met in his word. For them, plain walls are a form of reverence. But later in the same book, God tells Moses to make two cherubim of beaten gold for the cover of the ark. So images were not simply absent from Israel's worship. The Orthodox build on another verse. Paul calls Christ "the image of the invisible God." Their argument, made by John of Damascus when icons were under attack: the invisible God can't be painted. But when God became human, he could be seen and touched, and what can be seen can be pictured. So icons are honored, kissed and prayed before. The honor, they say, passes to the one shown; worship belongs to God alone. Catholics keep statues and paintings, crucifixes and stained glass, in a similar spirit: a picture as a way in, never the thing worshiped. Other Protestant churches sit in between, with a plain cross, a window, or a painting of the Last Supper. So the argument isn't really whether images are good or bad. Each church is guarding something: the commandment, or the God who became visible. And each is asking what helps people pray, and what gets in the way.

Let your eyes move slowly around the place where you pray, or where you go to be quiet: a cross, a candle, a photo, a window, a blank wall, or nothing at all. Ask of each thing: does this help me be still, or pull me somewhere else? Just notice, without changing anything; if you pray, ask God for whatever helps, and if you don't, let the looking be the practice.
Images. Icons, statues and pictures: honored by some churches as windows toward God, kept out by others to guard the commandment.
Your line: what helps you pray. Gold walls and white ones, both on purpose. See you next time.

1106.title: Purgatory and the dead
1106.hook: Catholics teach purification after death and pray for the dead; the Orthodox pray for the dead without that word; Protestants pray differently
1106.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead and have Masses offered for them, especially on All Souls' Day; Orthodox Christians hold memorial services and sing "memory eternal"; Protestant funerals commend the dead to God and give thanks for their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, images: icons, statues and plain white walls. Your line was what helps you pray.

Paul, writing to Timothy, remembers a man named Onesiphorus. When Paul was in chains in Rome, this man wasn't ashamed of him; he searched the city until he found him. Then Paul prays for him: "The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day." Paul greets the household of Onesiphorus, not the man himself, and some readers think he had already died. If so, this is Paul praying for the dead. What happens to those who have died is today's question.
screen: `A FRIEND WHO FOUND PAUL IN CHAINS.`
`MAY HE FIND MERCY IN THAT DAY.`

segments.voice: Catholics teach that some who die in God's grace are not yet fully ready to see God, and are purified after death. That purifying is called purgatory. It isn't a second chance, and it isn't a milder hell: those being purified are saved, and it ends in heaven. So Catholics pray for the dead, and have Masses offered for them. They point to Second Maccabees, a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. After a battle, Judas Maccabeus finds that fallen soldiers had carried idols, and he has prayers and a sacrifice offered so that their sin might be blotted out. They point, too, to Paul's picture of a builder whose work is tested by fire: "he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire." The Orthodox also pray for the dead, at memorial services where they sing memory eternal, and entrust them to God's mercy. But they don't use the word purgatory, or describe the state of the dead in the same detail. Protestant churches, following the Reformers, set purgatory aside. They teach that Christ's work is enough, and that those who die in him go to be with him. At Protestant funerals the dead are commended to God, and their lives given thanks for. This week walked through places where churches part ways: baptism, the table, Mary, the saints, images, and now the dead. On each, the differences are real, and honestly held. And under today's, Paul's short prayer for his friend still stands: may he find mercy.

Wait for a face to come, a grandparent, a friend, someone you never got to say goodbye to, and say their name; remember one ordinary thing, the way they laughed, the food they made. If you pray, commend them to God's mercy in your tradition's words; if you don't, hold their memory gently, and thank them. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Purgatory. In Catholic teaching, the purifying of the saved after death, before they see God. The Orthodox and Protestants speak of the dead in other ways.
Your line: mercy after death. A friend, remembered in a prayer. Rest well.

chat.says: My grandpa's church prays for the dead, and mine doesn't. Why?
options: Catholics and Orthodox pray for the dead; Protestants trust Christ's work is enough and give thanks.
Every church teaches purgatory now; some just pray for the dead more quietly than others.
Catholics pray for the dead because purgatory is a second chance to choose God after death.
chat.meaning: Catholics pray for those being purified; the Orthodox entrust the dead to God's mercy; Protestants teach Christ's work is enough, commending the dead to God with thanks.
